exam: A 4‑year‑old with HIV presents with new‑onset seizures – what immediate investigations and why? — Rapid malaria test, CSF analysis, and MRI to differentiate HIV‑HAND from cerebral malaria; treat seizures and start ART.

How does microglial activation differ in cerebral malaria versus TB meningitis? — Malaria triggers sequestration‑induced cytokine surge; TB causes granulomatous inflammation; CSF patterns and imaging help distinguish.

What bedside sign suggests raised intracranial pressure in a child with suspected microglial inflammation? — Papilledema on fundoscopy; indicates need for urgent neuro‑imaging or lumbar puncture deferment.
Why is dexamethasone contraindicated in viral encephalitis despite inflammation? — Steroids suppress immune clearance of virus and may worsen viral replication.
Explain the WHO HIV‑CNS staging and its impact on management. — Stages (asymptomatic to severe) guide timing of ART intensification and neuro‑rehabilitation intensity.

A child with severe malnutrition and cerebral malaria improves clinically but still has microglial activation on MRI – what is the next step? — Continue antimalarial therapy, start neuro‑rehab, monitor for post‑malaria neurocognitive sequelae.
How would you manage a child with suspected TB meningitis when GeneXpert is unavailable? — Start empiric anti‑TB regimen plus adjunctive dexamethasone; obtain CSF for cell count and protein.
What are the red‑flag features that mandate transfer to a higher‑level centre? — Status epilepticus, GCS ≤8, hydrocephalus, or inability to perform essential imaging.
ai.subject: Paediatrics
ai.summary: Microglia are the resident immune cells of the developing brain, acting as macrophages that shape neurodevelopment and respond to infection. In low‑resource settings they are central to HIV‑associated neurocognitive disorder and cerebral malaria. Recognising their role guides bedside assessment and targeted investigations.

b: Resident immune surveillance cells of the CNS
Become activated by infection, trauma, or neurodegeneration
sections.p: Microglial cells are specialised macrophage‑like cells derived from yolk‑sac progenitors that populate the brain early in gestation. They are identified histologically by Iba‑1 or CD68 staining, but clinically their activation is inferred from neuro‑imaging and CSF findings.

t.b: Does the scan show diffuse hyperintensity or focal lesions suggesting microglial activation? → Hyperintensity supports encephalitis or HIV‑associated neurocognitive disorder; normal scan makes primary metabolic disease more likely.

Is there pleocytosis or elevated protein indicating inflammatory activation? → ↑ white cells or protein supports infectious or inflammatory trigger; normal values do not exclude early microglial activation.

b: Mild: subtle cognitive delay, normal exam
Moderate: behavioural change, mild motor signs
Severe: seizures, coma, focal deficits
sections.p: In paediatric HIV‑associated neurocognitive disorder (HAND) microglial activation is staged by the WHO HIV‑CNS scale (asymptomatic, mild, moderate, severe). Cerebral malaria severity is graded by the WHO coma score.

b: HIV infection – microglia are a viral reservoir
Cerebral malaria (Plasmodium falciparum) – sequestration induces microglial inflammation
Tuberculous meningitis – granulomatous inflammation activates microglia
Severe bacterial meningitis (e.g., Streptococcus pneumoniae) – acute microglial response
Herbal or traditional remedies causing neurotoxicity
sections.p: In East African hospitals the common triggers of pathogenic microglial activation in children are:

b: Progressive cognitive decline or developmental regression
Behavioural changes (irritability, apathy)
Seizures or focal neurological signs
Headache, vomiting, papilledema in severe cases
sections.p: Clinical clues reflect the underlying disease but share a pattern of neuro‑inflammation:
Prioritise bedside‑available tools; when advanced imaging is lacking, use clinical algorithms.

t.b: Is Plasmodium falciparum present? → Positive test directs antimalarial therapy; negative test prompts search for other causes.
Is the child HIV‑positive? → Positive result explains microglial reservoir and guides ART initiation.

t.a: CSF Gram stain & GeneXpert MTB/RIF (if available)
t.b: Does CSF show bacterial organisms or MTB DNA? → Guides antimicrobial choice; if unavailable, treat empirically for bacterial meningitis.
Is papilledema present? → Suggests raised intracranial pressure from severe inflammation.

b: Persistent seizures or status epilepticus
Rapidly worsening coma (Glasgow ≤8)
Hydrocephalus on ultrasound
Severe malnutrition worsening neuro‑outcome
sections.p: Failure to control microglial‑driven inflammation can lead to irreversible brain injury.

b: Antiretroviral therapy (ART) for HIV – suppresses viral replication in microglia
Intravenous artesunate for cerebral malaria – rapidly clears parasites
Empiric ceftriaxone + vancomycin for bacterial meningitis – covers common pathogens
Adjunctive dexamethasone (where TB meningitis suspected) – reduces inflammatory edema
Neuro‑rehabilitation: physiotherapy, speech therapy, nutrition
sections.p: Treat the underlying trigger first, then modulate inflammation and support neuro‑recovery.

b: Monthly neuro‑developmental screening for the first year after treatment
Routine CD4 count and viral load for HIV‑positive children
Bed net use and prompt malaria treatment to prevent cerebral malaria
Vaccination against Haemophilus influenzae type b and pneumococcus
sections.p: Long‑term monitoring focuses on neurodevelopmental milestones and ART adherence.

b: Acute encephalitis (viral) – usually has fever and CSF lymphocytosis
Metabolic encephalopathies (e.g., hypoglycaemia) – reversible with metabolic correction
Neuro‑degenerative disorders (e.g., early‑onset Alzheimer) – slower progression
Normal CSF protein does not exclude early microglial activation
Negative malaria RDT can be false‑negative in low parasitaemia; consider thick smear
MRI may be unavailable; rely on clinical staging
